title: Analyzing Failure Modes in Semantic Role Labeling (SRL)
text:
The primary failure mode for Semantic Role Labeling occurs when the system encounters predicate-argument ambiguity rooted in lexical polysemy or metaphor. Since SRL attempts to map a fixed set of roles (e.g., Agent, Theme) onto observed linguistic spans, its success is fundamentally dependent on accurately determining the intended *sense* of the verb. If the predicate shifts meaning—for instance, interpreting 'launch' as a celestial event versus a product rollout—the assigned semantic frames will fail, resulting in incorrect role identification and scope boundaries.

Structural vulnerabilities also emerge when analyzing non-canonical sentence structures or those involving advanced coordination. Systems designed on canonical parsing assumptions struggle significantly with passive voice constructions where the Agent is omitted, complex ellipsis (missing arguments), or when embedded clauses complicate argument tracking. In these cases, standard constituency grammars may accurately parse the syntax but fail to semantically connect all necessary roles due to lack of explicit trigger phrases.

Furthermore, deep failures often involve distinguishing semantic scope and boundaries. When multiple constituents could plausibly fulfill an argument role (e.g., identifying which location serves as the 'Source' versus the primary 'Destination'), or when the desired role is inherently implicit or shared between roles (overlapping arguments), current SRL models face significant limits. The system must not only label a segment but also definitively demarcate its exact semantic contribution relative to the core predicate.
